summary: Noble held several IDIQ supply contracts with the Defense Logistics Agency (the FSG-53, FESE, PACOM MRO, and SOE contracts), most of which had already expired, been non-renewed, or been terminated for cause before Noble's bankruptcy filing, leaving thousands of delivery orders in various states of completion. After the August 30, 2026 petition date, DFAS (DLA's payment processor) placed an administrative hold on roughly $3.2 million (later shown to be about $6.97 million) in payments owed to Noble on prepetition invoices, in order to preserve the government's right to set off debts it says Noble owes it — chiefly a ~$7.9 million net FSG-53 performance disincentive and a ~$2.9-3.5 million False Claims Act settlement balance. Noble filed an emergency motion (Dkt. 102) to compel DLA to pay the held invoices and to enforce the automatic stay; the United States/DLA objected (Dkt. 124), arguing the contracts were not executory, the amounts were not yet due, and a creditor may temporarily withhold payment to protect a setoff right under Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf. After hearings on September 16 and 18, 2026, and after the parties failed to agree on a form of order (Dkt. 142), the Court ruled (Dkt. 151) that DLA's freeze had gone further than Strumpf allows and ordered DLA to release the improperly withheld funds, net of the undisputed settlement debt, while preserving DLA's right to seek stay relief later to litigate and exercise setoff over the remaining disputed amounts. On October 13, 2026, the dispute widened: DLA moved to lift the stay to formally terminate ~21,000 largely-dead delivery orders (hearing Oct 28), and the government separately disclosed a far larger False Claims Act exposure in two newly-unsealed qui tam suits — see the DOJ & FCA tab for the full breakdown.

timeline.event: Effective date of the FSG-53 Contract (an IDIQ contract encompassing five underlying DLA contract numbers), which included a 1-year transition period and a 3-year base ordering period (Oct. 2023-Sept. 2026) with unexercised option periods.

DLA notifies Noble that it will not exercise the FSG-53 Contract's first option period, effectively ending the ordering period as of September 30, 2026 (though completion of pending orders continues after that).

Noble (successor to Noble Sales Co., Inc.) executes a False Claims Act Settlement Agreement with the United States (DOJ/Dept. of the Air Force) related to a Cannon Air Force Base contract, agreeing to pay $1,034,495.99 plus 5% interest in six semi-annual installments.
FESE Contract ordering period expires after DLA declines to exercise the first option period; 150 delivery orders are later terminated for cause prepetition, 10 remain open.
PACOM MRO Contract and all its option periods expire; 1,217 delivery orders are later terminated for cause prepetition, 132 remain open.

First of three DLA notifications (also Aug. 17 and Sept. 1, 2026) to Noble of its intent to cancel a combined 11,893 outstanding FSG-53 delivery orders (of 20,380 outstanding as of the petition date); Noble did not object to the July/August notices, and the bankruptcy filing stayed DLA from formally modifying the contract to reflect the cancellations.

DLA issues notices of termination for cause on the SOE Contract, terminating it and 2,669 delivery orders; Noble indicated it intended to appeal under the Contract Disputes Act but, per DLA, had not filed a certified claim or appeal by mid-September.

Petition Date. DFAS has an administrative hold in place on payments due to Noble (under CAGE Code 1HEN9) for prepetition goods/services; held invoices total approximately $3,226,144.26 as of DLA's objection.

Debtors file an Emergency Motion (Dkt. 102) for an order compelling DLA to perform/pay under the contracts (~$3,226,144.26), enforcing the automatic stay, and ordering DLA to cease alleged stay violations.

United States, on behalf of DLA, files its Objection (Dkt. 124), arguing the contracts are not executory (IDIQ, expired/terminated), amounts are not yet due under the Prompt Payment Act, and the temporary hold is a lawful preservation of setoff rights under Strumpf given DLA's claims (net FSG-53 disincentive of $7,907,033.24 for Years 1-2, and an accelerated FCA settlement claim of $2,921,275.69 after 3 of 6 installments paid). First hearing held same day; a WAWF snapshot at 1:14 p.m. ET that day shows $6,972,618 owed across 879 invoices.

Unable to agree on a form of order after the hearing, the United States files a Certification of Counsel (Dkt. 142) attaching its own proposed order and a blackline against the Debtors' competing version; the U.S.'s proposed order would have released only $6,972,618 pending a further stay-relief/estimation process, subject to DLA's continued ability to reinstate blocks above a $10,290,636.04 payable threshold.

Second hearing held. The Court finds DLA's administrative freeze exceeded what Strumpf permits (it covered more than was reasonably necessary to protect DLA's setoff rights, and DLA never promptly sought a setoff order); orders DLA to pay Noble $6,972,618 (the amount improperly frozen) minus the $538,183.63 the Debtors acknowledge is owed on the FCA settlement, i.e. $6,434,434.37, within three business days. The Court also denies the United States' request for a stay pending appeal (or an administrative stay), citing Noble's urgent liquidity need to avoid conversion to chapter 7.

The United States (on behalf of DLA) files a Notice of Appeal (Dkt. 263) of the September 18 order (Dkt. 151) to the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware, seeking to overturn the ruling that DLA's payment freeze exceeded what Strumpf permits. The bankruptcy court already denied a stay pending appeal, so DLA's payment obligations under the September 18 order remain in effect while the appeal is pending.

The government's appeal is formally transmitted to, and docketed in, the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware as Civil Action No. 26-cv-1279-UNA (Bankruptcy Appeal No. 26-00059 / BAP No. 26-56). The filing fee was waived as the appellant is a government agency. Per standard local practice, the case is automatically referred to a U.S. Magistrate Judge to assess suitability for mediation before briefing begins; this is a routine procedural step, not a ruling on the merits. The bankruptcy court's September 18 order compelling DLA's payment remains in full effect pending the appeal (no stay was granted).

Noble files a new, separate adversary complaint against DLA (Adv. Proc., Docket #272) seeking turnover of at least $18,960,176.31 for 'Accepted Delivery Orders' — goods delivered and services provided that the government accepted but has not paid for. Noble alleges DLA is refusing to validate proof of delivery and is using the August 27, 2026 contract terminations as a blanket excuse not to pay, including for orders completed before the termination date. This is a new, larger dollar dispute than the $6.97M administrative-freeze fight resolved in the September 18 order (Docket #151) — that order is now on appeal (Civil Action No. 26-cv-1279-UNA) — and raises the total amount Noble is actively litigating against DLA to recover.

Noble files an emergency motion to expedite a motion for partial summary judgment in its new $18.96M turnover adversary proceeding against DLA (Adv. Proc. No. 26-50885, Docket #272). The Court schedules a status hearing just one day later, on October 8, 2026 at 4:00 PM ET via Zoom, to address the request.

DLA (via the United States) moves for limited relief from the automatic stay to formally terminate approximately 21,000 delivery orders under the largely-expired FSG-53, SOE and MRO contracts — nearly all past due or already agreed to be wound down — and to end Noble's obligation to staff an on-site supply store at a U.S. Army depot. DLA says none of these orders were completed or paid for; it is not seeking to claw back money, just to formally close out dead contracts. Hearing set for October 28, 2026 at 2:00pm ET; objections due October 21.

The United States moves for adequate protection of its setoff rights (a super-priority administrative claim plus a reserve from any sale proceeds), disclosing for the first time that it has partially unsealed two False Claims Act qui tam lawsuits against Noble (District of New Mexico and District of Massachusetts) and says total damages/penalties it believes Noble owes under those suits are no less than $266 million — far larger than the ~$7.9 million FSG-53 disincentive claim and ~$3.5 million settlement balance previously disclosed. The motion also confirms the United States formally objected on October 9 (Dkt. 297) to Noble's plan to assume/assign 100+ federal contracts at a $0 cure cost, and that Noble commenced its $18.96 million turnover adversary proceeding (Adv. No. 26-50885) on October 6, seeking expedited partial summary judgment.

Ahead of the October 16 final cash collateral hearing, the United States files a reservation of rights arguing the secured lenders' liens cannot be given greater priority than the Debtors' own rights, and that the Debtors' recoupment/setoff defenses against government claims survive regardless of lien priority; the Unsecured Creditors' Committee separately reserves its right to object to the final order if ongoing negotiations over its form and budget don't resolve its concerns.

The United States files its Statement of the Issues to Be Presented on Appeal (Docket #345) from the September 18 turnover order (Docket #151), formally identifying its appellate grounds (Civil Action No. 26-cv-1279-UNA) — including that the Bankruptcy Court erred in ordering the $6.43 million turnover via emergency motion instead of a formal adversary proceeding, in finding DLA's setoff rights adequately protected, and in its reading of Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf on administrative freezes. The government also files its designation of the record on appeal (Docket #346) the same day — a procedural step, not a new ruling.

The Debtors and the United States file witness-and-exhibit lists (Docket #397, #400) ahead of the October 28 omnibus hearing, confirming it will cover not just the stay-relief and adequate-protection motions but also Noble's motion for partial summary judgment, the government's motion to dismiss, and its cross-motion for summary judgment in the related adversary proceeding over DLA's ~$400 million SOE contract termination (Adv. Proc. No. 26-50885). The court separately notices that it wants the parties prepared to argue, at that same hearing, whether it has jurisdiction over Noble's breach-of-contract claim at all given the government's sovereign immunity — or whether the claim must instead be transferred to the U.S. Court of Federal Claims (Docket #407).

Debtors file their counter-designation of the record on appeal in the United States' appeal of the September 18 order (Docket #151) to the U.S. District Court (Civil Action No. 26-cv-01279-JLH), adding the transcript of the October 28, 2026 hearing and the three interim cash-collateral orders to the appellate record.

The Court issues a 48-page Memorandum Opinion (Docket #427) resolving Noble's $18.96 million turnover adversary proceeding together with the government's Stay Relief and Adequate Protection Motions. The Court grants partial summary judgment for Noble, ordering the government to pay $8,493,160.09 on undisputed matured invoices by November 9, 2026, while dismissing without prejudice the portion of Noble's turnover claim tied to disputed delivery destinations. Implementing orders follow at Docket #422 (stay relief granted) and #424 (adequate protection denied).

outcome: A partial, court-imposed resolution that leaned in Noble's favor on the immediate cash-flow issue but preserved DLA's underlying setoff claims for later litigation. Judge Goldblatt granted the Debtors' emergency motion 'to the extent set forth' in the order: he ruled that DLA's blanket administrative freeze on Noble's payables exceeded what Citizens Bank of Maryland v. Strumpf permits (DLA could have paid amounts coming due without prejudicing its setoff rights, and unlike the creditor in Strumpf, DLA never promptly moved for setoff relief). The Court ordered DLA to pay Noble $6,434,434.37 within three business days — the $6,972,618 in improperly frozen payables, netted against the $538,183.63 Noble concedes it owes under the FCA settlement agreement. Going forward, DLA must pay Noble in the ordinary course and cannot reinstate any freeze or exercise setoff/replacement rights without first obtaining stay relief from the Court; if DLA believes future payables are not adequately protecting its claims (e.g., the disputed ~$7.9 million FSG-53 disincentive claim), it may file a stay-relief motion, and the Court will conduct a Section 502(c) estimation proceeding to size the competing claims. The order was effective immediately, and the Court denied the government's request for a stay pending appeal given Noble's urgent liquidity needs.
financial_stakes: Administrative hold on Noble's prepetition invoices: initially described as ~$3,226,144.26 (per the Debtors' motion and DLA's objection), but the WAWF-verified figure at the time of the September 16 hearing was $6,972,618 across 879 invoices — the amount the Court ultimately found had been improperly frozen. Net amount the Court ordered DLA to actually remit: $6,434,434.37 (after offsetting the undisputed FCA settlement debt). Offsetting claims asserted by DLA/the United States: (1) a net FSG-53 performance disincentive of $7,907,033.24 for Years 1-2 (Year 1 disincentive $8,303,730.26 less Year 2 incentive $396,697.02; Year 3 not yet calculated); (2) an accelerated False Claims Act settlement claim, cited as $2,921,275.69 in DLA's objection but resolved at $538,183.63 (per the Sept. 18 order) / $537,672.89 (per the Sept. 17 competing proposed order) as the amount actually owed and setoff in this ruling, out of an original $3,481,737.91 accelerated-default claim. Note: no figures resembling a ~$400 million contract termination or an ~$86 million claim appear anywhere in the dockets reviewed (0124, 0142, 0151) — the disincentive, settlement, and administrative-hold amounts above are the only dollar figures the DLA payment-freeze dispute documents disclose. NEW (Oct 13, 2026): the government separately disclosed a far larger False Claims Act exposure — two newly-unsealed qui tam suits with claimed damages/penalties of no less than $266 million — in a motion seeking adequate protection of its setoff rights. That figure, and the government's related requests, are covered in full on the DOJ & FCA tab.
